title: "Estimating the 2PL in torch: which estimator closes the gap to mirt?"
description: |
  The network comparison on the companion page found that a torch 2PL trails the
  `mirt` 2PL by a small but consistent margin. Here we take that margin apart. We
  fit the 2PL four ways in torch (gradient descent, alternating joint maximum
  likelihood, EM, and direct maximisation of the marginal likelihood), with and
  without a constraint that fixes the scale of the person parameters, and score
  each against `mirt` on the same 24 IRW tables. The estimator explains the gap;
  the scale constraint does not.

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| code-summary: "Setup"
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch
from nn_irt_helpers import TABLES, SHORT, DATA, prepare, fit, log_loss, make_models
from imvpy import vanilla_imv
from IPython.display import display

Rasch, TwoPL, Bilinear, MLP = make_models()
torch.set_num_threads(4)
plt.rcParams["figure.dpi"] = 110
```

## Motivation

The [companion page](nn_irt.qmd) fits a 2PL in PyTorch and compares it with the
`mirt` 2PL on 24 tables. The torch model is slightly worse on most of them, and
the margin is largest on the short tests. Two things differ between the two fits,
and the companion page could not separate them. One is how the scale of the
person parameters is set: the PyTorch 2PL puts a penalty on $\theta$, while
`mirt` fixes its population variance by assumption. The other is the estimator:
the PyTorch model is fit by gradient descent on the joint likelihood, with each
person's $\theta$ treated as a parameter, while `mirt` integrates the persons out.

This page separates the two. Every estimator below is fit to the same training
cells and scored on the same held-out cells, and each is compared with `mirt` by
the InterModel Vigorish.

## The estimators

Each estimator is a different way of fitting the same 2PL, $\operatorname{logit}
P(y_{pi}=1) = a_i\theta_p + d_i$. Two of them come from the prior-or-constraint
choice for the scale, and two from the estimator choice.

- **Adam, prior.** Minibatch gradient descent on the joint log-likelihood plus
  an $N(0,1)$ penalty on each $\theta_p$, stopped at the best held-out epoch.
  This is the companion page's network.
- **Adam, constrained.** The same network with $\theta$ standardised across
  persons in the forward pass, so it has mean zero and SD one by construction,
  and no penalty.
- **Alternating JML, prior.** Joint maximum likelihood by block updates: with
  the items fixed, a Newton step for every person's $\theta_p$ (with the
  $N(0,1)$ penalty, so this is alternating MAP); with the persons fixed, a Newton
  step for every item's $(a_i, d_i)$. Repeat.
- **Alternating JML, constrained.** The same block updates without the penalty.
  After each person update $\theta$ is standardised, and the scale is moved into
  $a$ and $d$, which leaves the fitted probabilities unchanged.
- **EM, marginal maximum likelihood.** The estimator `mirt` uses. The E-step
  gives each person a posterior over a quadrature grid, given their training
  cells; the M-step fits each item's $(a_i, d_i)$ by weighted logistic regression
  on the grid. Held-out cells get the posterior-predictive probability.
- **MML, L-BFGS.** Start from 200 EM iterations, then maximise the marginal
  likelihood directly with `torch.optim.LBFGS` and autograd. Same model and
  objective as EM; a different optimiser for the last step.

Joint and alternating estimators predict with the point estimates of $\theta_p$
(plug-in). EM and MML predict with the posterior. The Adam networks stop at their
best held-out epoch, and the alternating JML fits stop at their best held-out
sweep, which is the same rule and the same caveat: the held-out set also picks
the stopping point.

## The scale is fixed weakly by the penalty

The prior version fixes the scale of $\theta$ only through the penalty. In the
likelihood $a_i\theta_p$ is the only thing that matters, so the same fit can be
written with a small $\theta$ and a large $a$, and the penalty pulls
$\theta$ toward zero at a constant price. Alternating JML makes the drift easy to
see. The run below uses no early stopping and records the person SD and the median
slope every 100 sweeps on the residency exam.

```{python}
#| label: fig-drift
#| code-summary: "Scale drift in the prior version of alternating JML"
drift = pd.read_csv(DATA / "drift_borges_alt_jml.csv")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.6))
ax[0].plot(drift.sweep, drift.theta_sd, color="#2a78d6")
ax[0].set(xlabel="sweep", ylabel=r"SD of $\hat\theta$", title="person SD")
ax[1].plot(drift.sweep, drift.median_a, color="#eb6834")
ax[1].set(xlabel="sweep", ylabel="median slope $a$", title="item slopes")
for a_ in ax:
    for sp in ("top", "right"):
        a_.spines[sp].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(drift.iloc[[0, 1, 5, 10, -1]].round(4).to_string(index=False))
```

Over 2000 sweeps the person SD falls from 0.55 to 0.04 and the median slope rises
from 1.1 to 13. The held-out log-loss does not move, 0.5482 from sweep 100 to sweep 2000, because $a\theta$ is what the likelihood sees and it is nearly fixed while
the two factors slide against each other. A penalty that weak does not
identify the scale. The constrained version fixes it exactly, and that is the
only difference between the two alternating fits.

## Results: each estimator against mirt

Each row is one table. The columns give the IMV of the `mirt` 2PL over each
estimator, so a positive number means `mirt` predicts the held-out cells better
than that estimator does.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-estimators
#| code-summary: "IMV of mirt 2PL over each estimator, all tables"
rows, stops = [], []
for t in TABLES:
    d = prepare(t)
    te = d[d.test]
    m = te[["id", "item"]].merge(pd.read_csv(DATA / f"{t}_mirt_preds.csv.gz", dtype={"id": str, "item": str}),
                                 on=["id", "item"], how="left")
    mirt = m["mirt_2pl"].values
    e = pd.read_csv(DATA / f"{t}_estimation_preds.csv.gz")
    tp = pd.read_csv(DATA / f"{t}_torch_preds.csv.gz")
    y = e.y.values
    est = {"Adam prior": tp["2PL"].values, "Adam constr.": tp["2PL (constr.)"].values,
           "JML prior": e["alt JML (prior)"].values, "JML constr.": e["alt JML (constr.)"].values,
           "EM": e["EM MML"].values, "MML L-BFGS": e["MML L-BFGS"].values}
    r = {"table": SHORT[t]}
    for k, p in est.items():
        r[k] = vanilla_imv(p, mirt, y)
    r["max |diff| MML"] = np.abs(est["MML L-BFGS"] - mirt).max()
    rows.append(r)
    info = pd.read_csv(DATA / f"{t}_estimation_info.csv")
    jml = info[info.estimator.str.startswith("alt JML")]
    for _, q in jml.iterrows():
        stops.append({"table": SHORT[t], "estimator": q.estimator, "best_sweep": q.best_sweep,
                      "stopped": q.stopped})
res = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("table")
summary = res.mean().rename("mean over tables")
out = pd.concat([res.round(4), summary.round(4).to_frame().T])
out
```

```{python}
#| label: jml-stops
#| code-summary: "Where the alternating JML fits stopped"
S = pd.DataFrame(stops)
print(S.groupby(["estimator", "stopped"]).size().unstack(fill_value=0).to_string())
print()
print(S.groupby("estimator")["best_sweep"].describe()[["50%", "max"]].to_string())
```

Three things stand out.

**The torch MML matches mirt.** The L-BFGS fit, which maximises the same marginal
likelihood `mirt` does, is within 0.0001 of `mirt` on average, and the EM fit
within 0.0012. The two largest disagreements are on the ASQ and Denver
screeners and on EDSC, where several items are nearly perfectly separated by the
persons, so their parameters sit at magnitudes in the hundreds and the likelihood
is very flat along them. On the ASQ and Denver screeners the torch fit has the
higher marginal likelihood of the two. These are numerical differences on
ill-determined items, and they do not change the picture: the same model,
estimated by maximising the same objective, gives the same predictions.

**The gap is the estimator.** The torch networks trail `mirt` by 0.005 on
average when they are fit by Adam and by 0.008 when they are fit by alternating
JML, and the MML fit closes the gap to about zero on the same tables. Optimiser
quality is not the explanation either: the EM and L-BFGS fits both converge, and
they agree with each other. What differs is whether the person parameters are
integrated out or treated as known. That is the difference the companion page
pointed to, and this page confirms it by reproducing `mirt` once the integration
is in place.

**Alternation does not help.** Alternating joint maximum likelihood is the
textbook way to fit a joint model, and it is worse than the Adam fit on average,
0.008 against 0.005 for the prior version and 0.018 against 0.007 for the
constrained one. The reason is the one the incidental-parameter problem
predicts. The held-out log-loss of the alternating fit is lowest within the first
few sweeps on most tables. The best sweep falls within the first ten on 22 of
24 tables for the prior version and on all 24 for the constrained one (medians
three and two), and the constrained fit stopped on the patience rule rather
than convergence on 18 tables. On the shorter tests the loss rises after that: on the COVID knowledge test it
goes from 0.690 at sweep one to 0.81 by sweep ten and to 0.98 for the
constrained version by sweep twenty, as some items separate the persons and their
slopes run away. The held-out stopping rule then returns an estimate from the
first few sweeps on those tables. The constrained fit is worst on the Onah test,
with 20 training responses per person, where the gap to `mirt` is 0.185.

## Constraining the scale

The constrained versions are the other half of the question. Fixing $\theta$ at
$N(0,1)$ removes the drift above, and the next figure checks whether it also
recovers the item parameters on the residency exam. The `mirt` estimates are the
reference. The top row is the prior version, scaled by the spread of
$\hat\theta$; the bottom row is the constrained version, whose spread is one by
construction.

```{python}
#| label: fig-recovery
#| code-summary: "Item parameters: prior and constrained 2PL against mirt"
t = "borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt"
d = prepare(t)
ref = pd.read_csv(DATA / f"{t}_mirt_2pl_items.csv", dtype={"item": str})
ref = ref.set_index("item").reindex(sorted(d["item"].unique()))
n_p, n_i = int(d.pid.max() + 1), int(d.iid.max() + 1)
fits = {"prior": fit(TwoPL(n_p, n_i), d)[0], "constrained": fit(TwoPL(n_p, n_i, constrained=True), d)[0]}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(9, 8))
for row, (label, net) in enumerate(fits.items()):
    sd_theta = net.theta.weight.detach().numpy().std()
    scale = sd_theta if label == "prior" else 1.0
    a_hat = net.a.weight.detach().numpy().ravel() * scale
    d_hat = net.d.weight.detach().numpy().ravel()
    ax[row, 0].scatter(ref.d, d_hat, s=12)
    ax[row, 0].set(xlabel="mirt 2PL intercept $d$", ylabel=f"PyTorch intercept $d$ ({label})")
    ax[row, 1].scatter(ref.a, a_hat, s=12)
    ax[row, 1].set(xlabel="mirt 2PL slope $a$", ylabel=f"PyTorch slope $a$ ({label})")
    for a_ in ax[row]:
        lo, hi = a_.get_xlim(); a_.plot([lo, hi], [lo, hi], "k--", lw=0.8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The intercepts agree closely in both versions, and the slopes agree after the
scale is handled, with the constrained slopes about 9% above `mirt`'s and the
rescaled prior slopes about 3% above. The constraint does what it is meant to:
the scale is set, and nothing is left to drift.

The constraint does not, however, close the gap in prediction, and on the
networks it costs something. The table compares every network in both versions
with the prior 2PL, which is the zero line, as on the companion page.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-constrained
#| code-summary: "Constrained versus prior, every network, IMV against the prior 2PL"
rows = []
for t in TABLES:
    d = prepare(t)
    y = d[d.test].resp.values
    tp = pd.read_csv(DATA / f"{t}_torch_preds.csv.gz")
    base = tp["2PL"].values
    r = {"table": SHORT[t]}
    for name in ["Rasch", "2PL", "MIRT k=2", "MLP small", "MLP large"]:
        r[f"{name}"] = vanilla_imv(base, tp[name].values, y)
        r[f"{name} (constr.)"] = vanilla_imv(base, tp[f"{name} (constr.)"].values, y)
    rows.append(r)
res = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("table")
out = pd.concat([res.round(4), res.mean().rename("mean over tables").round(4).to_frame().T])
out
```

The constrained Rasch is the clearest case. It is worse than the prior Rasch on
every one of the 24 tables, by 0.03 on average and by 0.19 on the Onah test. The
prior Rasch lets the data set the spread of $\theta$: it comes out at 0.56 on the
residency exam and 0.40 on the Onah test, so the penalty does not hold the scale
at one. The constraint forces one, and the Rasch model has no slope to absorb the
difference. The 2PL pays almost nothing for the same constraint, because its
slopes can take up the scale. The wider networks are close to unchanged on
average, with the constrained MIRT and MLPs within about 0.003 of the prior
versions, but with losses on the short tests (the listening test, the Ding
knowledge test and the psychTools ability test).

The constraint does not stop the wide networks from overfitting, either. The
figure refits the prior and constrained networks on the residency exam, for 30
epochs each, and plots held-out loss by epoch.

```{python}
#| label: fig-curves
#| code-summary: "Held-out loss by epoch, prior and constrained, residency exam"
from nn_irt_helpers import nn_specs
curves = {}
for con in (False, True):
    for name, mk in nn_specs(n_p, n_i, con).items():
        _, h = fit(mk(), d, epochs=30)
        curves[name + (" (constr.)" if con else "")] = h
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
for k, (name, h) in enumerate(c for c in curves.items() if not c[0].endswith("(constr.)")):
    ax.plot(h.epoch, h.test, color=f"C{k}", label=name)
    ax.plot(curves[name + " (constr.)"].epoch, curves[name + " (constr.)"].test, color=f"C{k}", ls="--")
ax.set(xlabel="epoch", ylabel="held-out log-loss", title="solid: prior; dashed: constrained")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, frameon=False)
for sp in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The wide networks reach their best held-out loss early, and they climb after it
in both versions. The constrained MIRT and large MLP bottom out at epochs five and
eight and then climb by about 0.005 and 0.006. The constrained 2PL stays flat, as
the prior one does. So fixing the scale changes how the scale is set, not whether
the wide networks memorise their training cells, and early stopping is still what
keeps them honest.

## Limitations

- **Two estimators are on a common footing; the networks are not.** The MML fits
  are the same model as `mirt` and are compared directly. The Adam networks and
  the alternating JML fits are different estimators of the same model, and their
  gaps to `mirt` are gaps in estimation, not in the model.
- **Stopping uses the held-out set.** The Adam networks and both alternating JML
  fits pick their stopping point on the held-out cells, which flatters them
  slightly. The MML fits do not use held-out data at all: they maximise the training
  likelihood (EM, then four L-BFGS rounds).
- **Items with extreme parameters.** On the ASQ, Denver and EDSC screeners several
  items have parameters in the hundreds, and the marginal likelihood is flat along
  them. Two correct maximisers can stop at different points there, which is why
  the largest MML disagreements with `mirt` are on those tables.
- **Dichotomous 2PL only.** The estimators here are for the 2PL on 0/1 responses,
  and the multidimensional and nonlinear networks are not refit with them.

## Reproducibility

**Source code for this page:**
[`nn_irt_estimation.qmd`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_estimation.qmd),
[`nn_irt_estimation.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_estimation.py),
[`nn_irt_estimation_compute.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_estimation_compute.py)
and [`nn_irt_estimation_drift.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_estimation_drift.py),
with the network fits in [`nn_irt_helpers.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_helpers.py).

The estimator comparison and the drift trace are cached in
`vignettes/nn_irt_data/` (`*_estimation_preds.csv.gz`, `*_estimation_info.csv`,
`drift_borges_alt_jml.csv`), with the MML and Adam predictions and the `mirt`
predictions from the companion page. The figures that refit a network do so on
the residency exam at the page's seed, so they re-render without the caches. To
regenerate the caches:

```bash
# 1. Adam networks, both versions, all tables (companion page's cache)
python vignettes/nn_irt_torch_compute.py
# 2. The 2PL three further ways on all tables, plus the drift trace
python vignettes/nn_irt_estimation_compute.py
python vignettes/nn_irt_estimation_drift.py
# 3. The offline mirt predictions (companion page)
Rscript vignettes/nn_irt_mirt_compute.R
# 4. Re-render this page
quarto render vignettes/nn_irt_estimation.qmd
```
